source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the nurse's own explanatory model consistently so treatment decisions are not altered by differing cultural beliefs about mental illness.","B":"Explore the client's beliefs and preferences, incorporate them into collaborative care when feasible, and avoid stereotyping the individual.","C":"Assume clients from the same cultural group share the same beliefs, then select treatment according to the group's expected preferences.","D":"Avoid discussing cultural beliefs because biomedical treatment is most effective when personal explanatory models are excluded from care."}}
source_row.rationale: Culturally sensitive mental health care includes understanding and respecting the client's own cultural beliefs about mental illness, its causes, and appropriate treatment approaches (which may differ significantly across cultures), integrating this understanding into a collaborative, individualized care approach — while also recognizing individual variation within any cultural group rather than assuming uniformity.
source_row.source_detail: National CLAS Standards, Principal Standard: respectful, understandable, quality care responsive to cultural health beliefs/practices, preferred languages, health literacy, and other communication needs. Current HHS Think Cultural Health standards reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: APA — Cultural Competence in Mental Health Care Guidelines
source_row.stem: A nurse is providing mental health care to a client whose cultural background has different beliefs about mental illness than the nurse's own, and the nurse initially wonders whether it would be simpler to just apply their own clinical framework rather than navigate the difference.
